clue.text: Campaign ad covers front of office in maroon

indicators.note: one thing covering another hides it from view, so the ad stands in place of the letter it sits on

parts.note: a maroon is a person left on a desert island, and Robinson Crusoe is the most famous one

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of office
taken as written

explanation.surface: An advertising campaign is lavished on an office painted dark red.
explanation.walkthrough: Maroon looks like a colour, but here it is the rare noun for a castaway; swap the O in CRUSOE for AD.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade is a vigorous organised campaign for a cause, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Comic of little value new, cents tops

indicators.note: in a down answer, what tops the rest sits above it, at the start

parts.note: c is the abbreviation for cents
low means of little worth
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A cheap new comic book costing a few cents at most.
explanation.walkthrough: Comic looks like a magazine in the surface, but it is a person who makes people laugh.
explanation.definitionFit: A clown is a comic performer, someone who acts the fool to amuse.

clue.text: One holding 26 up, edition not bound

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a unit is a single one

indicators.note: in a down answer, going up means reading from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: the answer to 26-down
ed is the abbreviation for edition

explanation.surface: A limited edition copy of a book, still unbound, is held up.
explanation.walkthrough: In a bookish setting 'edition not bound' suggests a paperback, but 'not bound' is the definition, meaning unrestricted.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlimited means without restriction, free of any bounds or limits.

clue.text: Some drama fellow misplaced in non-fiction

indicators.note: something misplaced has gone missing, so that letter is lost from the word

parts.note: fact is the opposite of fiction
F is the abbreviation for fellow

explanation.surface: A man who wandered into the factual section by mistake causes a little drama.
explanation.definitionFit: An act is one of the main divisions of a play, so it is a portion of drama.

clue.text: Feeling upset by large bestseller in 16?

indicators.note: in a down answer, set upside down means the letters are read from the bottom up

parts.note: a number one in a book shop, the top seller, with I as the numeral one
a tome is a large heavy book, the bestseller in question

explanation.surface: An author is distressed by a hefty bestseller on the bookshop shelves.
explanation.walkthrough: The bestseller is a large book: a number one tome. 16 refers to 16-down's answer, BOOKSHOPS.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a feeling, such as joy or anger, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: For leaves, Flora of South Africa

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
tea is the dried leaves of the tea plant

explanation.surface: A botanist notes the leaves of the plants of South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The protea is a South African flowering plant, the country's national flower, so it is an example of its flora.

clue.text: Dickensian lad starts to explain chimney-sweeping, thinner brush for narrow flue

parts.note: Pip is the boy hero of Dickens's Great Expectations

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, the only ones taken

parts.note: the opening letters of explain and chimney-sweeping
leaner means slimmer, thinner

explanation.surface: A Dickensian boy chimney-sweep explains that a thinner brush suits a narrow flue.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a Victorian climbing boy, but the narrow flue is the stem of a tobacco pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe cleaner is a thin bristled wire for cleaning the narrow stem of a smoker's pipe.

clue.text: Fantastic Mr Fox making robbery primarily a charitable enterprise

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful and unreal, so the letters are reworked freely
making something into something else turns it into another thing, so one letter becomes another

parts.note: the title character's name taken letter by letter

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is meant

parts.note: the opening letter of robbery
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dahl's Fantastic Mr Fox, a story of farmyard theft, as a charity project.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the R of MR FOX into A, then rearrange. Fantastic Mr Fox is a Roald Dahl title, so its first word hides the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxfam is a large British charity, which also runs many second-hand shops.

clue.text: Carriage returns, queen collecting Notes From a Small Island

indicators.note: collecting things means gathering them in, so the notes go inside

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword shorthand for the Queen
N for note plus te, a note of the sol-fa scale
a key is a low small island, so of a key reads KEY'S

explanation.surface: Royal carriages come back with the Queen reading Bill Bryson's Notes From a Small Island.
explanation.walkthrough: Carriage returns are the keyboard keys that start a new line, nothing to do with horse-drawn coaches.
explanation.definitionFit: On a computer keyboard the enter key does the job of the typewriter's carriage return.

clue.text: T S Eliot disturbed retiree in bar with perfume

indicators.note: something disturbed has been thrown out of its settled order, so the poet's name gets rearranged

parts.note: the poet's name taken letter by letter
OAP, old-age pensioner, is the British term for a retired person

explanation.surface: The poet T S Eliot is upset by a pensioner in a pub wearing too much scent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub in the surface, but it is a bar of soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet soap is the scented kind sold in bars for washing, so a perfumed bar describes it.

clue.text: Mates Scott and Gerald divided by the sound of it

indicators.note: we are told to judge by how the word is pronounced, not how it is spelt

parts.note: in the writer F Scott Fitzgerald's name, Fitz separates Scott from Gerald

explanation.surface: A literary note on the two Scotts and Geralds, friends who were split up.
explanation.walkthrough: Mates is a verb here, as in 'this lid mates with the jar'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit is to match or join up with something, which is what a part mating with another does.

clue.text: Dictator embraced by the French, after revolution — Napoleon, according to Orwell

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the result is read backwards
being embraced means being held inside arms, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: la is French for the, feminine form
Idi Amin was the dictator of Uganda

explanation.surface: A dictator taken in by the French after the Revolution suggests Napoleon, as judged by Orwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon seems to be the French emperor, but in Orwell's Animal Farm he is the pig who becomes dictator.
explanation.definitionFit: In Animal Farm Napoleon is a pig, so for Orwell he is a farm creature.

clue.text: Pound for one Allende with a line crossed through, right money

indicators.note: putting a crossbar through the stem of a capital letter changes its shape into a different letter

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pound
eg, for example, means for one
the surname of Chilean novelist Isabel Allende
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A pound, say, given to Allende is crossed off, and right money.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross the second L of ALLENDE with a horizontal stroke and it becomes a T. Pound looks like an example of the definition, but it is the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal tender is money that must be accepted in payment of a debt, coins and notes.

clue.text: New visitor mad on crime

indicators.note: something mad is out of its right mind and order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the two words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A fresh arrival in town is crazy about crime.
explanation.definitionFit: An incomer is a person newly arrived in a place, a newcomer rather than a native.

clue.text: African leaves End of Watch by King, old volunteers taken aback

indicators.note: placed beside, so one piece is set next to the other

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of watch

indicators.note: aback means backwards, so these letters run from right to left

parts.note: the TA, Territorial Army, was the British volunteer reserve force, now renamed

explanation.surface: Stephen King's novel End of Watch, about old volunteers, is taken from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: End of Watch is a real Stephen King title, which disguises 'End of' as part of a book name.
explanation.definitionFit: Khat is an East African shrub whose leaves are chewed as a stimulant.

clue.text: Staff paid nothing worked safely without touching

parts.note: hands are workers, the staff
something free costs nothing

explanation.surface: Unpaid staff worked carefully and never laid a finger on anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A hands-free device, such as a car phone kit, is operated without being held, which is safer when driving.

clue.text: Greene and half of Brighton rock to 17's pop

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so the letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: the novelist Graham Greene's surname

indicators.note: half a word is one of its two halves, here the opening one

parts.note: the first four of the eight letters of Brighton

explanation.surface: Graham Greene's novel Brighton Rock seems to be the subject, compared to a children's author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Brighton Rock is a Greene novel and a seaside sweet, but 'rock' is the anagram signal. Pop is a fizzy drink, and 17 is the children's author in 17-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger beer is a fizzy soft drink famously linked to the Famous Five stories, so it is that author's pop.

clue.text: Some 6 outlets smell, certainly hot inside concessions

indicators.note: one thing inside another sits within it

parts.note: BO, body odour, is an unpleasant smell
OK as an answer means yes, certainly
sops are small concessions made to placate someone
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Some charity outlets do smell, and the concession stands are very hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 refers to 6-down's answer, OXFAM, whose shops include many selling second-hand books.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxfam runs dedicated bookshops among its many charity stores, so some of its outlets are of this kind.

clue.text: Tiny blonde novel writer criticised for being dumb

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the two words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A petite fair-haired novelist is attacked for being stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun describing a book, but it is the anagram signal; dumb here means dumbed down.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid Blyton, the prolific children's author, was long criticised for her simple vocabulary and limited style.

clue.text: Second-hand dealer's wobbles when walking

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a totter is a British rag-and-bone man, a scrap dealer; with 's for the possessive
second meaning: moves unsteadily on one's feet

explanation.walkthrough: A totter is a rag-and-bone man, a dealer in scrap and old goods, as in TV's Steptoe and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a possessive of a scrap collector and a verb for staggering unsteadily along.

clue.text: Part of France which Esio Trot's first name comes from?

indicators.note: Dahl's title is a word spelt backwards, so its source is found by turning it round

parts.note: the first word of Roald Dahl's book title Esio Trot

explanation.surface: A playful question about where the title of Roald Dahl's book Esio Trot comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Esio Trot is tortoise written backwards, so its first word came from the end of tortoise.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oise is a department of northern France, named after its river.

clue.text: Das Boot typed with thumbs? It's not obvious to the reader

definitions.text: It's not obvious to the reader

parts.note: Das Boot is the German film about a submarine, a sub
a phone message is tapped out with the thumbs

explanation.surface: Someone thumbs out a message about the war film Das Boot, though its meaning is unclear.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtext is the meaning beneath the surface of a text, something a reader must infer.

clue.text: Security instruments of The Spy Who Loved Me

definitions.meaning: first meaning: certificates of debt issued by a government or company

definitions.text: of The Spy Who Loved Me
definitions.note: a phrase meaning belonging to the spy defines the possessive Bond's, which sounds and reads the same as the plural noun
definitions.meaning: second meaning: belonging to James Bond, hero of that Fleming title

explanation.walkthrough: The Spy Who Loved Me is a James Bond novel and film, so 'of' it is Bond's.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonds are tradeable financial securities, while Bond's is the possessive of the fictional spy James Bond.

clue.text: Person in a hurry read out scene of War and Peace

indicators.note: reading out means speaking the words, so we go by their pronunciation

parts.note: one who rushes

explanation.surface: Someone hastily reading aloud a passage from Tolstoy's War and Peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolstoy's War and Peace is set in Russia during the Napoleonic invasion.

clue.text: Island with butcher, Whisky Galore there

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island
to butcher is to slaughter, slay

explanation.surface: An island with a butcher, the setting of the film Whisky Galore.
explanation.walkthrough: Whisky Galore looks like the Compton Mackenzie title, but it means lots of whisky: Islay is famous for its many distilleries.
explanation.definitionFit: Islay is a Hebridean island packed with distilleries, a place of plentiful Scotch.

clue.text: One of Elements, and not one Through the Looking Glass

indicators.note: a mirror shows writing back to front, so the letters are read in the opposite order

parts.note: nor means and not
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Book titles: one of Euclid's Elements, and not one of Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass.
explanation.walkthrough: Elements and Through the Looking-Glass look like book titles, but one is the chemical elements and the other a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron is a metallic chemical element, number 26 in the periodic table.

clue.text: Doctor Marlowe fashioned, leading character in devilish fantasy

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor

indicators.note: something fashioned has been shaped anew, so the playwright's letters are remade

parts.note: the playwright's name taken letter by letter

indicators.note: the leading character of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of devilish

explanation.surface: Marlowe's Doctor Faustus is created, its lead character in a diabolical fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor and Marlowe together evoke Doctor Faustus with its devil, but Doctor just gives the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamworld is an imaginary, unreal realm, the stuff of fantasy.

clue.text: A Brontë's inside small volume

indicators.note: the inside of a word is everything bar its outer letters

parts.note: Emily Brontë, minus her first and last letters

explanation.surface: One of the Brontë sisters appears within a slim book.
explanation.walkthrough: Mil is informal for millilitre, as in '250 mil of water'.
explanation.definitionFit: A millilitre is a tiny measure of liquid, so it is a small volume.

clue.text: Time to relax with reading/writing puzzle

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to ease is to relax
reading and writing are two of the three Rs, each written as R

explanation.surface: Time to unwind with some reading or a writing puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, so either of the first two is an R.
explanation.definitionFit: A teaser, short for brain-teaser, is a tricky problem or riddle.

clue.text: Whip in The Secret Agent for show

indicators.note: placed in means sitting inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
a lash is a whip

explanation.surface: A whip appears in Conrad's novel The Secret Agent purely for effect.
explanation.walkthrough: The Secret Agent is a Joseph Conrad novel title, but here it just means a spy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something splashy is showy and ostentatious, done to attract attention.
